Start at 45: around MUR 26,000/month needed
steps.note: Retirement poverty is real — and almost entirely preventable with early, consistent action.

steps.title: How the Mauritius pension system works
steps.body:
Mauritius has two main pension layers built into the system.

The Basic Retirement Pension is a universal payment available to all citizens at retirement age — regardless of employment history. The National Pension Fund is a contributory scheme where you and your employer both contribute a percentage of your salary throughout your working life.

steps.title: What NPF actually provides
steps.body:
The NPF builds up over your working years through mandatory contributions. At retirement, it pays you a monthly income based on your contribution history.

For most people, the NPF and BRP together cover the basics — housing costs, food, essential utilities. They rarely cover the lifestyle most people expect to maintain into retirement.

steps.title: Building your own layer on top
steps.body:
Beyond the state system, you can build personal retirement wealth through several paths.

Approved private pension schemes offer tax-deductible contributions. Long-term savings and investment accounts grow independently. Property can generate rental income in retirement. A diversified investment portfolio can be drawn down gradually.

The more sources you have, the more resilient your retirement becomes.

steps.title: Do not rely on one source
steps.body:
The state system protects everyone from the worst outcomes. But a comfortable retirement requires more than the minimum.

Every contribution you make to your own pension or investments during your working years reduces the gap between what the state provides and what you actually need.
bullets: BRP: universal state pension — available to all at retirement age
NPF: contributory scheme — builds with your salary deductions
Personal savings: your own layer — needs to be built deliberately
steps.note: Do not rely solely on the state pension. Build your own retirement fund alongside the mandatory contributions.

steps.title: The most powerful financial decision you can make
steps.body:
Of all the factors that determine how much wealth you retire with — income, savings rate, investment choices — time is the most powerful by a significant margin.

A person who starts saving at twenty-two and stops at thirty-two can accumulate more than someone who saves from thirty-two to sixty-two — even though the second person contributes three times as much money.

steps.title: Why the numbers work this way
steps.body:
Compounding means that returns are reinvested, and then earn returns themselves. Over decades, the growth becomes exponential rather than linear.

In the early years, it looks slow. In the middle years, it looks steady. In the later years, it accelerates dramatically. The ten-year head start captures the most powerful part of that curve.

steps.title: What small amounts actually become
steps.body:
MUR 500 per month from age twenty-two, invested at eight percent annual return.

By forty: approximately MUR 290,000. By fifty: approximately MUR 700,000. By sixty: approximately MUR 1,600,000.

MUR 500 a month is the price of a few meals out. Over forty years, it becomes over a million and a half rupees.

steps.title: You cannot buy back time
steps.body:
You can always earn more. You can always save a higher percentage. You can always find a slightly better investment.

But you cannot go back in time and start earlier. Every year of delay costs you a compounding cycle you cannot recover.
bullets: Starting at 22 vs 32 matters more than doubling your savings rate
Even MUR 300 to 500 a month, started early, becomes significant
The best time to start was earlier. The second best time is now.
steps.note: Starting early is the single most powerful retirement decision available to you.

steps.title: How much will you actually need?
steps.body:
A common estimate is that most people need around seventy to eighty percent of their pre-retirement income to maintain their lifestyle in retirement.

Work expenses disappear. Mortgage payments may be finished. But healthcare typically increases. Leisure spending often stays. The overall number is lower than your working income — but not dramatically so.

steps.title: How to calculate your personal target
steps.body:
Start with your desired monthly retirement income. Subtract whatever you expect to receive from the state pension. The gap that remains is what your personal savings need to cover.

Multiply that annual gap by twenty-five. That is your savings target — based on the principle that withdrawing four percent of a well-invested portfolio per year is sustainable over a long retirement.

steps.title: A worked example
steps.body:
You want MUR 30,000 a month in retirement. Your expected pension covers MUR 10,000.

Personal savings need to cover MUR 20,000 a month — MUR 240,000 a year.

MUR 240,000 multiplied by twenty-five: your savings target is MUR 6,000,000.

Divide that by the number of years until retirement to find your annual contribution target. Then divide by twelve to get the monthly amount.

steps.title: The number is less scary when it is broken down
steps.body:
MUR 6,000,000 feels enormous. But MUR 4,000 a month for thirty-five years, at reasonable investment returns, gets you there — and that is before factoring in employer contributions or any additional savings.

The goal is not to save MUR 6,000,000 at once. It is to build toward it, one month at a time.
bullets: Desired monthly income minus expected pension = monthly gap
Multiply annual gap by 25 to find total savings target
Divide by years remaining to get your monthly contribution target
steps.note: Calculate your number. Then build a plan around it — starting as early as possible.

steps.title: Security is built in layers, in order
steps.body:
Long-term financial security is not the result of one good decision. It is the result of many consistent decisions, made in the right order over many years.

The order matters. Trying to invest before you have an emergency fund means one bad month forces you to sell investments. Paying for lifestyle upgrades before clearing high-interest debt costs you years.

steps.title: The order that works
steps.body:
Phase one: build the emergency fund and clear high-interest debt. These protect you from the financial shocks that derail everything else.

Phase two: maximise pension and retirement contributions. Time is still on your side here — every year you contribute earlier compounds significantly.

Phase three: build an investment portfolio beyond retirement. Diversify across assets.

Phase four: protect everything you have built with appropriate insurance.

steps.title: The quiet threat: lifestyle inflation
steps.body:
As income grows, there is a natural pull to spend more. A bigger flat. A newer car. More dining out. More subscriptions.

None of this is wrong — but doing it automatically, without intention, is how people earn significantly more than they used to and still feel like they are not getting ahead.

The habit that changes this: every time your income increases, direct at least half of the increase to savings or investments before adjusting your lifestyle.

steps.title: What consistent decisions actually produce
steps.body:
Thirty years of modest, consistent decisions — saving a percentage every month, investing regularly, avoiding high-interest debt, maintaining insurance — produce outcomes that feel extraordinary to people who never started.

Not because they required sacrifice every day. Because they compounded quietly in the background while life went on.
bullets: Protect first: emergency fund and insurance before everything else
Grow consistently: invest every month regardless of amount
Resist lifestyle inflation: save half of every raise before spending it
steps.note: Small, consistent decisions over thirty years produce outcomes that look dramatic — because compounding is exponential.
